75	**(c) Fair Market Value Determination.** For purposes of this Article IV, \"Fair Market Value Per Share\" means the fair market value of one Share as of the date of the Transfer Notice, as determined by an independent appraiser mutually agreed upon by the Transferring Stockholder and the Company. The independent appraiser shall be a qualified valuation firm with experience in the valuation of privately held life sciences companies. If the Transferring Stockholder and the Company cannot agree on an independent appraiser within ten (10) business days following the Transferring Stockholder\'s request for determination, then each of the Transferring Stockholder and the Company shall, within five (5) business days thereafter, select one independent appraiser, and the two appraisers so selected shall, within ten (10) business days of their appointment, select a third independent appraiser. The determination of the Fair Market Value Per Share by such third appraiser shall be final, binding, and non-appealable. The costs and expenses of the appraisal process shall be borne equally by the Company and the Transferring Stockholder, except that each party shall bear the costs of the appraiser it selects in the event the three-appraiser process described above is invoked.

77	**Section 4.3 --- Drag-Along Rights.**
78	
79	**(a) Drag-Along Obligation.** If the holders of a majority of the outstanding Shares (determined on a fully diluted, as-converted basis) (the \"Dragging Stockholders\") approve a bona fide sale of the Company (a \"Drag-Along Sale\"), whether structured as a merger, consolidation, recapitalization, sale of all or substantially all of the assets of the Company, sale of all outstanding Shares, or any other transaction or series of related transactions resulting in a Change of Control (as defined in Article I), then each other Stockholder (each, a \"Dragged Stockholder\") shall be required to:
80	
81	> \(i\) vote all of such Dragged Stockholder\'s Shares in favor of the Drag-Along Sale and refrain from exercising any dissenters\' rights, appraisal rights, or similar rights available under applicable law;
82	>
83	> \(ii\) tender or transfer such Dragged Stockholder\'s Shares on the same terms and conditions as the Dragging Stockholders, including as to price per share, form of consideration, representations, warranties, covenants, indemnification obligations, and escrow or holdback arrangements, provided that no Dragged Stockholder shall be required to provide representations and warranties other than as to such Dragged Stockholder\'s title to and ownership of its Shares, authority, and absence of conflicts, or to bear indemnification obligations in excess of the aggregate proceeds received by such Dragged Stockholder in the Drag-Along Sale; and
84	>
85	> \(iii\) execute and deliver all agreements, instruments, certificates, and documents reasonably requested by the Dragging Stockholders or the acquirer in connection with the consummation of the Drag-Along Sale.
86	
87	**(b) Notice.** A written notice of a Drag-Along Sale (a \"Drag-Along Notice\") shall be delivered to all Dragged Stockholders not less than twenty (20) business days prior to the proposed closing date of the Drag-Along Sale. The Drag-Along Notice shall set forth the material terms and conditions of the Drag-Along Sale, including the identity of the acquirer, the consideration to be received, and the anticipated closing date.

As a condition to any Transfer of Shares to a trust, the trust instrument of such trust must include provisions expressly binding the trustee (and any successor trustee) to comply with this Section 4.3, including the obligation to vote, tender, and transfer the trust\'s Shares in any Drag-Along Sale. 22	
23	**[Section 1: Engagement Overview and Purpose]{.underline}**
24	
25	Ridgeline Valuation Group, LLC (\"Ridgeline\" or the \"Firm\") was engaged by Helios Biosciences, Inc. (\"Helios\" or the \"Company\") to determine the fair market value of one share of the Company\'s common stock as of March 31, 2025 (the \"Valuation Date\") for purposes of compliance with Internal Revenue Code (\"IRC\") Section 409A. The valuation was requested to support the Company\'s stock option pricing and equity compensation programs and to ensure that equity-based awards are granted at exercise prices that meet or exceed the fair market value of the underlying common stock on the date of grant, as required by IRC §409A and the regulations promulgated thereunder.
26	
27	In addition to its primary purpose of supporting IRC §409A compliance, this report may be used by shareholders of the Company and their authorized advisors for estate and gift tax planning purposes, including but not limited to the valuation of gifts of common stock or the funding of grantor retained annuity trusts and similar transfer vehicles. Such use is subject to the assumptions and limiting conditions described in Section 9 of this report. Users should note that the applicable standard of value for federal gift tax purposes under IRC §2512 is the same as the standard applied herein.
28	
29	Ridgeline is an independent valuation firm and has no ownership interest in Helios Biosciences, Inc. The Firm\'s compensation for this engagement is based on customary professional fees and is not contingent in any manner upon the conclusions reached or the amount of the value determined. Ridgeline has no financial interest in the Company and no economic relationship with the Company or its shareholders that would impair the Firm\'s objectivity or independence.
30	
31	David Ashworth, ASA, CFA, served as the principal analyst for this engagement and is responsible for the analyses, opinions, and conclusions stated herein. Mr. Ashworth\'s qualifications are summarized in Section 10 of this report.
32	
33	The subject of this valuation is the common stock of Helios Biosciences, Inc., a Delaware C-corporation founded in 2009 and headquartered at 275 Science Park Drive, New Haven, CT 06511. The Company is engaged in the development and commercialization of novel therapeutics for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
34	
35	The standard of value applied in this report is **fair market value**, as defined under IRC §409A and Treasury Regulation §1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B), which provides that fair market value is \"the price at which property would change hands between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither being under any compulsion to buy or sell and both having reasonable knowledge of relevant facts.\" This same standard of value applies under IRC §2512 for federal gift tax purposes and under IRC §2031 for federal estate tax purposes. Our concluded fair market value is stated on a minority, non-marketable interest basis, reflecting the characteristics of a share of common stock held by a non-controlling shareholder in a privately held company with no established public trading market.
36	
37	**[Section 2: Company Description]{.underline}**
38	
39	**Corporate Overview.** Helios Biosciences, Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation founded in 2009 by Dr. Priya Chandrasekaran, along with two co-founders, Dr. Marcus Elliot and Dr. Naomi Yashiro. The Company is headquartered at 275 Science Park Drive, New Haven, CT 06511, where it maintains its principal offices and research laboratories. Bramwell & Associates serves as the Company\'s corporate counsel.
40	
41	**Business Description.** Helios is a privately held biopharmaceutical company focused on the development and commercialization of novel therapeutics for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. The Company\'s platform technology is based on targeted immune modulation, and its pipeline includes both small-molecule and biologic candidates addressing conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and inflammatory bowel disease. The Company was pre-revenue until 2018, when it began receiving milestone payments and licensing royalties from its first commercialized product. As of the Valuation Date, Helios generates annual revenue of approximately \$67 million from a combination of product sales, milestone payments received under collaboration agreements, and licensing royalties. The Company occupies a competitive position within the mid-cap biopharmaceutical sector, with a robust and diversified pipeline of candidates at various stages of clinical development.
42	
43	**Revenue Trajectory.** Helios was in its development stage from its founding through 2018, during which period the Company generated no significant product revenue. Beginning in fiscal year 2019, the Company commenced recognizing revenue from its first commercialized therapeutic product and from licensing arrangements with pharmaceutical partners. Revenue has grown meaningfully since that time, reaching approximately \$67 million in the most recent fiscal year, demonstrating a trajectory of accelerating growth that reflects both expanding product sales and the maturation of the Company\'s pipeline.
44	
45	**Capitalization Summary.** As of the Valuation Date, the Company\'s capital structure consists of common stock and outstanding stock options. The total number of shares of common stock outstanding as of March 31, 2025 was 7,800,000. In addition, the Company has outstanding stock options (both vested and unvested) that, on a treasury stock method basis, represent an additional 835,000 dilutive shares. Accordingly, the fully diluted share count as of the Valuation Date is **8,635,000 shares**. The Company does not have any outstanding preferred stock as of the Valuation Date.
46	
47	**Ownership.** Dr. Priya Chandrasekaran holds 1,560,000 shares of common stock, representing approximately 18.1% of the Company\'s fully diluted shares. Other shareholders include the Company\'s co-founders, early employees and advisors who received equity grants, and institutional investors who participated in prior financing rounds. No single shareholder holds a majority of the Company\'s outstanding equity.
48	
49	**Transfer Restrictions.** The Company\'s Amended and Restated Stockholders\' Agreement (the \"Stockholders\' Agreement\") contains significant restrictions on the transferability of common stock. Section 4.2 of the Stockholders\' Agreement requires board consent for any transfer of shares to trusts or similar estate planning vehicles. In addition, the Stockholders\' Agreement provides a 30-day right of first refusal (\"ROFR\") at fair market value in favor of the Company and certain existing shareholders on any proposed transfer of shares. Section 4.3 of the Stockholders\' Agreement also contains drag-along provisions that may be triggered upon a qualifying sale transaction. These restrictions were considered in the application of valuation discounts, as discussed in Section 7 below.
50	
51	**Recent Developments Through the Valuation Date.** As of March 31, 2025, the Company maintains an active pipeline with multiple clinical-stage programs. Helios has several collaboration and licensing agreements in place with larger pharmaceutical partners, which provide milestone payments and royalty streams. The Company\'s financial position as of the Valuation Date is reflected in the selected financial data presented in Appendix B. Market conditions in the biopharmaceutical sector as of the Valuation Date were generally favorable, with continued investor interest in companies with validated immune-modulation platforms. Management reported no material adverse developments or pending litigation as of the Valuation Date.
52	
53	**[Section 3: Valuation Methodology]{.underline}**
54	
55	In performing this valuation, Ridgeline considered three standard approaches to business valuation as prescribed by the American Society of Appraisers and the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice: (1) the Income Approach, (2) the Market Approach, and (3) the Asset/Cost Approach. The selection of appropriate valuation methodologies was based on the nature of the Company, the availability and reliability of relevant data, and the specific characteristics of the subject interest.
56	
57	**Income Approach --- Discounted Cash Flow (DCF).** The Income Approach, specifically the Discounted Cash Flow method, was selected as the primary methodology and was assigned a weighting of **60%** in the final reconciliation of value. Under the DCF method, the enterprise value of the Company is estimated as the present value of its expected future free cash flows, discounted at a rate that reflects the risk associated with those cash flows. This approach is particularly appropriate for a growth-stage biopharmaceutical company such as Helios that has a demonstrable revenue track record, a well-defined business model, and detailed financial projections provided by management. The DCF method captures the intrinsic value of the Company\'s expected growth trajectory and is well suited to reflect the value of future milestone payments, product sales growth, and pipeline monetization.
58	
59	**Market Approach --- Comparable Public Company Analysis (Guideline Public Company Method).** The Market Approach, specifically the Guideline Public Company Method, was selected as the secondary methodology and was assigned a weighting of **40%**. Under this method, valuation multiples derived from the market trading data of publicly traded companies with comparable business characteristics are applied to the financial metrics of the subject company to derive an indication of enterprise value. Ridgeline identified a sufficient number of publicly traded biopharmaceutical companies with comparable business profiles, development stages, and revenue characteristics to provide meaningful market-based valuation benchmarks. The Market Approach provides an independent, market-derived indication of value that serves as a useful check on the DCF analysis.
60	
61	**Comparable Transaction Analysis.** Ridgeline considered the Comparable Transaction Analysis under the Market Approach but elected not to rely upon it in this engagement. Insufficient data was available on recent private transactions involving biopharmaceutical companies at a stage comparable to Helios. The transactions that were identified occurred under circumstances that were not sufficiently comparable or involved terms that were not adequately disclosed to permit meaningful analysis.
62	
63	**Asset/Cost Approach.** The Asset/Cost Approach was considered but not selected for this engagement. The Company\'s value is derived primarily from its intellectual property portfolio, its product pipeline, its established collaboration agreements, and its going-concern operations. These intangible assets and growth prospects are not adequately captured by a net asset value methodology, which would significantly understate the Company\'s true economic value.
64	
65	**Weighting Rationale.** The 60% / 40% weighting assigned to the DCF and Guideline Public Company methods, respectively, reflects the relative reliability and applicability of each approach given the characteristics of Helios. The DCF method received greater weight due to the availability of detailed management projections spanning a five-year forecast period and the critical importance of growth expectations in determining the value of a company at this stage of development. The Guideline Public Company method received a meaningful secondary weight because it provides an objective, market-derived benchmark that reduces reliance on management\'s subjective projections.
66	
67	**[Section 4: Income Approach --- Discounted Cash Flow Analysis]{.underline}**
68	
69	**Projection Period.** The DCF analysis utilizes a five-year projection period covering fiscal years 2025 through 2029, based on financial projections provided by the management of Helios. These projections reflect management\'s expectations regarding revenue growth from existing products and pipeline candidates, the timing and magnitude of anticipated milestone payments under existing collaboration agreements, margin expansion as the Company achieves greater scale, and expected capital expenditure and working capital requirements. Beyond the explicit five-year projection period, a terminal value was calculated to capture the going-concern value of the Company\'s operations in perpetuity.
70	
71	**Key Assumptions.** The management-provided projections assume continued revenue growth from the Company\'s current product portfolio, supplemented by anticipated milestone payments and royalty streams from existing collaboration agreements. Revenue growth rates are projected to decline gradually over the projection period as the Company matures, from approximately 18% in fiscal year 2025 to approximately 9% by fiscal year 2029. Gross margins are expected to expand modestly as the Company\'s revenue mix shifts toward higher-margin product sales and royalty income. EBITDA margins are projected to improve from approximately 15% in fiscal year 2025 to approximately 22% by the end of the projection period, reflecting operating leverage and disciplined cost management. Capital expenditure requirements are expected to remain moderate relative to revenue, with annual capital expenditures ranging from approximately 4% to 6% of revenue over the projection period to support pipeline development and facility expansion. Net working capital needs are projected to increase in line with revenue growth.
72	
73	**Discount Rate.** The discount rate applied in the DCF analysis is the Company\'s estimated weighted average cost of capital (\"WACC\"), which was determined to be **15.25%**. The WACC was developed using the build-up method, incorporating the following components: a risk-free rate of 4.25% based on the yield on 20-year U.S. Treasury securities as of March 31, 2025; an equity risk premium of 5.50% based on published historical and forward-looking equity risk premium estimates; a size premium of 2.75% reflecting the Company\'s size relative to the broader equity market, consistent with published size premium data for micro-cap and small-cap companies; and a company-specific risk premium of 2.75% reflecting risks unique to Helios, including its dependence on a limited number of products and collaboration partners, its private company status, and the inherent risks associated with pharmaceutical development and regulatory approval. The Company\'s capital structure was assumed to consist entirely of equity, as the Company\'s relatively modest debt level does not materially affect the WACC calculation.
74	
75	**Terminal Value.** The terminal value was calculated using the Gordon Growth Model (perpetuity growth model), applying a long-term sustainable growth rate of **3.0%** to the Company\'s normalized free cash flow in the terminal year (fiscal year 2029). This long-term growth rate reflects expectations for the general economy, the biopharmaceutical sector, and the Company\'s competitive position. The terminal value was discounted to present value using the same 15.25% WACC.
76	
77	**Enterprise Value Indication.** Based on the DCF analysis, the indicated enterprise value of Helios Biosciences, Inc. as of the Valuation Date is approximately **\$190,000,000** (One Hundred Ninety Million Dollars). This figure represents the sum of the present value of projected free cash flows during the explicit five-year projection period and the present value of the terminal value.
78	
79	**Sensitivity Analysis.** The concluded DCF enterprise value is sensitive to changes in the discount rate and terminal growth rate assumptions. A 100 basis point increase in the WACC (to 16.25%) would reduce the DCF-indicated enterprise value by approximately \$12 million to \$14 million, while a 100 basis point decrease (to 14.25%) would increase the indicated enterprise value by a comparable amount. Similarly, a 50 basis point change in the terminal growth rate assumption would affect the indicated enterprise value by approximately \$6 million to \$8 million. These sensitivities underscore the importance of the assumptions underlying the DCF analysis and are within a range that Ridgeline considers reasonable.
80	
81	**[Section 5: Market Approach --- Comparable Public Company Analysis]{.underline}**
82	
83	**Guideline Companies.** Ridgeline identified seven publicly traded biopharmaceutical companies that serve as guideline comparables for purposes of the Market Approach. These companies were selected based on their comparability to Helios with respect to business focus (autoimmune, inflammatory, or immune-modulation therapeutics), stage of development (commercial-stage with established revenue), revenue scale, pipeline breadth, and market positioning. The following guideline companies were selected:
84	
85	> 1\. **Aethon Pharma, Inc.** --- A commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on autoimmune therapeutics, with annual revenues of approximately \$94 million and a diversified pipeline of small-molecule and biologic candidates.
86	>
87	> 2\. **Corvexa Life Sciences, Inc.** --- A specialty pharmaceutical company developing and commercializing therapies for inflammatory and fibrotic diseases, with annual revenues of approximately \$52 million.
88	>
89	> 3\. **Novalith Therapeutics, Inc.** --- A biopharmaceutical company focused on targeted immune modulation, with annual revenues of approximately \$78 million and multiple marketed products.
90	>
91	> 4\. **Purebridge Biomedical Corp.** --- A biopharmaceutical company with a platform technology in immune-oncology and autoimmune disease, with annual revenues of approximately \$61 million.
92	>
93	> 5\. **Solvanta Health, Inc.** --- A commercial-stage biopharmaceutical company with a primary focus on inflammatory bowel disease therapeutics, with annual revenues of approximately \$43 million.
94	>
95	> 6\. **Veridian BioSystems, Inc.** --- A diversified biopharmaceutical company developing targeted therapies for autoimmune and rare diseases, with annual revenues of approximately \$112 million.
96	>
97	> 7\. **Calyx Pharmaceuticals, Inc.** --- A biopharmaceutical company focused on novel biologic therapeutics for rheumatologic and inflammatory conditions, with annual revenues of approximately \$55 million.
98	
99	**Valuation Multiples Selected.** Ridgeline analyzed two primary valuation multiples derived from the guideline companies\' market trading data as of or near March 31, 2025: enterprise value to revenue (EV/Revenue) and enterprise value to EBITDA (EV/EBITDA). The observed ranges and selected multiples applied to Helios are summarized in the detailed comparable company data table in Appendix C. After considering the relative comparability of each guideline company to Helios, Ridgeline selected an EV/Revenue multiple of 2.55x and an EV/EBITDA multiple of 16.5x for application to Helios\'s financial metrics. These selected multiples fall within the interquartile range of the observed guideline company multiples and reflect adjustments for differences in growth rate, profitability, and risk profile between Helios and the guideline companies.
100	
101	**Application to Helios.** Applying the selected EV/Revenue multiple of 2.55x to Helios\'s trailing twelve-month revenue of approximately \$67 million yields an enterprise value indication of approximately \$171 million. Applying the selected EV/EBITDA multiple of 16.5x to Helios\'s trailing twelve-month EBITDA of approximately \$11.2 million yields an enterprise value indication of approximately \$185 million. Ridgeline reconciled these two indications, giving greater weight to the EV/Revenue multiple given its broader applicability and reduced sensitivity to margin variations among the guideline companies, and concluded a Market Approach enterprise value indication of approximately **\$177,500,000** (One Hundred Seventy-Seven Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars).
102	
103	**Adjustments.** In selecting the applicable multiples and concluding the Market Approach enterprise value, Ridgeline considered qualitative and quantitative differences between Helios and the guideline companies, including differences in revenue scale, growth rates, profitability margins, pipeline depth, and risk characteristics. The guideline companies are publicly traded and therefore benefit from greater liquidity and market visibility; however, this distinction is addressed through the application of valuation discounts in Section 7 rather than through adjustments to the Market Approach enterprise value.
104	
105	**[Section 6: Enterprise Value Reconciliation and Conclusion]{.underline}**
106	
107	Based on the analyses described in Sections 4 and 5, Ridgeline reconciled the enterprise value indications from the two selected valuation approaches using the weighting methodology described in Section 3.
108	
109	  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
110	  **Valuation Approach**                       **Indicated Enterprise Value**   **Weight**        **Weighted Value**
111	  -------------------------------------------- -------------------------------- ----------------- --------------------
112	  Income Approach (DCF)                        \$190,000,000                    60%               \$114,000,000
113	
114	  Market Approach (Guideline Public Company)   \$177,500,000                    40%               \$71,000,000
115	
116	  **Concluded Enterprise Value**                                                                  **\$185,000,000**
117	  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
118	
119	The concluded enterprise value is **\$185,000,000** (One Hundred Eighty-Five Million Dollars).
120	
121	**Bridge to Equity Value.** To derive the total equity value of the Company, Ridgeline adjusted the concluded enterprise value for the Company\'s net debt position as of the Valuation Date:
122	
123	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
124	  **Item**                            **Amount**
125	  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
126	  Concluded Enterprise Value          \$185,000,000
127	
128	  Less: Total Debt                    (\$18,500,000)
129	
130	  Plus: Cash and Cash Equivalents     \$6,200,000
131	
132	  Net Debt Adjustment                 (\$12,300,000)
133	
134	  **Implied Total Equity Value**      **\$172,700,000**
135	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
136	
137	**Per-Share Equity Value (Pre-Discount).** The per-share equity value on a marketable, controlling-interest basis is calculated by dividing the implied total equity value by the fully diluted share count:
138	
139	> Implied Total Equity Value: \$172,700,000 Fully Diluted Share Count: 8,635,000 shares Per-Share Equity Value: \$172,700,000 ÷ 8,635,000 = \$19.9942 ≈ **\$20.00 per share** (rounded)
140	
141	This per-share equity value of **\$20.00** represents the value of one share of common stock of Helios Biosciences, Inc. on a **marketable, controlling-interest basis**. This value does not reflect the characteristics of a minority, non-marketable interest and is presented prior to the application of the valuation discounts discussed in Section 7. The application of appropriate discounts for lack of marketability and lack of control is necessary to derive the fair market value of a share held by a non-controlling shareholder in a privately held company.
142	
143	**[Section 7: Valuation Discounts]{.underline}**
144	
145	**[7.1 Discount for Lack of Marketability (DLOM)]{.underline}**
146	
147	Helios Biosciences, Inc. is a privately held company. There is no established public trading market for the Company\'s common stock, and shareholders who wish to dispose of their shares face significant practical and contractual barriers to doing so. The Company\'s Stockholders\' Agreement imposes transfer restrictions, including a requirement of board consent for transfers to trusts or similar estate planning vehicles (Section 4.2) and a 30-day right of first refusal in favor of the Company and existing shareholders on any proposed transfer of shares. These restrictions, together with the general illiquidity inherent in shares of a private company, reduce the value of a share relative to a freely tradable share of an otherwise comparable publicly traded company.
148	
149	Ridgeline estimated the DLOM using a combination of three widely accepted empirical and theoretical frameworks:
150	
151	> \(1\) **Restricted Stock Studies.** These studies analyze the price discounts observed in private placements of restricted (unregistered) shares of publicly traded companies relative to the freely traded shares of the same issuer. The average discounts observed in these studies generally range from 20% to 35%, depending on the study and the time period analyzed, with a median in the range of approximately 25% to 30%.
152	>
153	> \(2\) **Pre-IPO Studies.** These studies compare the prices at which shares of companies were sold in private transactions prior to their initial public offerings with the IPO offering prices. The discounts observed in pre-IPO studies tend to be higher than those observed in restricted stock studies, reflecting additional factors such as uncertainty regarding the timing and success of the IPO.
154	>
155	> \(3\) **Option Pricing Models.** Ridgeline applied a put-option pricing model (based on the Finnerty model) to estimate the theoretical cost of illiquidity for Helios common stock, considering the expected holding period before a potential liquidity event, the estimated volatility of the Company\'s equity, and the risk-free rate.
156	
157	In selecting the DLOM, Ridgeline considered the following factors specific to Helios: the absence of any near-term anticipated liquidity event (such as an IPO or sale of the Company); the contractual transfer restrictions in the Stockholders\' Agreement; the Company\'s size and financial performance; the Company\'s lack of a dividend payment history; and the general absence of a secondary market for the Company\'s shares.
158	
159	Based on the foregoing analysis, Ridgeline concluded a Discount for Lack of Marketability of **25%**.
160	
161	Applying the 25% DLOM to the pre-discount per-share equity value:
162	
163	> \$20.00 × (1 − 0.25) = \$20.00 × 0.75 = **\$15.00 per share** (after DLOM, before DLOC)
164	
165	**[7.2 Discount for Lack of Control (DLOC)]{.underline}**
166	
167	The shares being valued represent a minority interest in Helios Biosciences, Inc. No individual minority shareholder --- including Dr. Chandrasekaran, who holds approximately 18.1% of the fully diluted shares --- can unilaterally control the Company\'s operations, management decisions, dividend policy, timing of a liquidity event, or other significant corporate actions. A hypothetical willing buyer of a minority block of common stock would expect to pay less than a pro rata share of the Company\'s total enterprise value because the buyer would have no ability to influence or compel corporate actions that would maximize the value of the investment.
168	
169	Ridgeline estimated the DLOC by reference to two principal sources:
170	
171	> \(1\) **Control Premium Studies.** Published studies of acquisition premiums paid in public company acquisitions indicate that acquirers typically pay a premium over the pre-announcement trading price to obtain a controlling interest. The inverse of the observed control premium provides an indication of the discount applicable to a minority interest. Observed control premiums in relevant sectors generally range from 20% to 40%, implying minority interest discounts in the range of approximately 15% to 30%.
172	>
173	> \(2\) **Company-Specific Factors.** Ridgeline considered the specific governance and ownership characteristics of Helios, including the concentration of ownership among the founders, the board composition, the drag-along provisions in Section 4.3 of the Stockholders\' Agreement (which could compel minority shareholders to participate in a qualifying sale transaction), and the presence of institutional investors who hold significant minority positions.
174	
175	Dr. Chandrasekaran\'s 18.1% ownership stake, while representing a significant minority position, does not confer control over the Company. The existence of drag-along rights and other protective provisions in the Stockholders\' Agreement further limits the practical control exercisable by any individual minority shareholder.
176	
177	Based on the foregoing analysis, Ridgeline concluded a Discount for Lack of Control of **10%**.
178	
179	Applying the 10% DLOC to the post-DLOM per-share value:
180	
181	> \$15.00 × (1 − 0.10) = \$15.00 × 0.90 = **\$13.50 per share**
182	
183	Alternatively, the combined discount application may be expressed as follows:
184	
185	> \$20.00 × (1 − 0.25) × (1 − 0.10) = \$20.00 × 0.75 × 0.90 = **\$13.50 per share**
186

from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Inches, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement

def new_doc():
    d = Document()
    sec = d.sections[0]
    sec.left_margin = sec.right_margin = Inches(1)
    sec.top_margin = sec.bottom_margin = Inches(1)
    st = d.styles['Normal']
    st.font.name = 'Times New Roman'
    st.font.size = Pt(12)
    st.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'), 'Times New Roman')
    st.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(6)
    for h in ['Heading 1','Heading 2','Heading 3']:
        s = d.styles[h]
        s.font.name = 'Times New Roman'
        s.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(0,0,0)
        s.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'), 'Times New Roman')
    d.styles['Heading 1'].font.size = Pt(13)
    d.styles['Heading 2'].font.size = Pt(12)
    d.styles['Heading 3'].font.size = Pt(12)
    # page numbers
    p = sec.footer.paragraphs[0]
    p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    r = p.add_run()
    for t,txt in [('begin',None),(None,'PAGE'),('end',None)]:
        if t:
            e = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); e.set(qn('w:fldCharType'), t); r._r.append(e)
        else:
            e = OxmlElement('w:instrText'); e.set(qn('xml:space'),'preserve'); e.text = txt; r._r.append(e)
    return d

def add_runs(p, text):
    # **bold** and _[italic note]_ markup: segments split by '**'
    parts = text.split('**')
    for i, part in enumerate(parts):
        if not part: continue
        sub = part.split('~~')
        for j, s in enumerate(sub):
            if not s: continue
            r = p.add_run(s)
            if i % 2 == 1: r.bold = True
            if j % 2 == 1: r.italic = True
    return p

def para(d, text, align=None, indent=None, bold=False, size=None, space_after=None, first=None):
    p = d.add_paragraph()
    add_runs(p, text)
    if bold:
        for r in p.runs: r.bold = True
    if size:
        for r in p.runs: r.font.size = Pt(size)
    if align == 'c': p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    elif align == 'j': p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.JUSTIFY
    elif align == 'r': p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
    if indent is not None: p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Inches(indent)
    if first is not None: p.paragraph_format.first_line_indent = Inches(first)
    if space_after is not None: p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space_after)
    return p

def shade(cell, hexcolor):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement('w:shd'); shd.set(qn('w:val'),'clear'); shd.set(qn('w:color'),'auto'); shd.set(qn('w:fill'),hexcolor)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def table(d, rows, widths=None, header=True, size=9.5):
    t = d.add_table(rows=len(rows), cols=len(rows[0]))
    t.style = 'Table Grid'
    for i,row in enumerate(rows):
        for j,val in enumerate(row):
            c = t.cell(i,j)
            c.text = ''
            p = c.paragraphs[0]
            add_runs(p, str(val))
            for r in p.runs:
                r.font.size = Pt(size)
                if header and i==0: r.bold = True
            p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(0)
            if header and i==0: shade(c,'D9D9D9')
            if widths: c.width = Inches(widths[j])
    d.add_paragraph()
    return t
EOF

ISSUE(1,'The funding value is overstated: \$20.00 is a pre-discount figure','Critical','Ridgeline Summary ' + chr(167) + chr(167) + '6' + chr(8211) + '8; Intake ' + chr(167) + chr(167) + 'I, IV.C, V.C; Engagement Letter; Silveroak Summary rows 29' + chr(8211) + '38 and Caveat 2; Estate Plan Summary ' + chr(167) + 'VIII',
 ['The intake memo, the engagement letter, the estate plan summary and the Silveroak workbook all treat \$20.00 per share as \"the per-share fair market value\" and fix funding at \$8,000,000. That is wrong. Ridgeline' + chr(8217) + 's \$20.00 is the equity value per share on a **marketable, controlling-interest basis** (\$172.7M equity / 8,635,000 fully diluted shares = \$19.9942). Section 8 of the report states that \$20.00 \"should not be used as a measure of the fair market value of minority shares without the application of appropriate discounts.\" A 400,000-share block (4.6% of fully diluted, 5.1% of outstanding) is a minority interest.   'Consequences: (a) on Ridgeline' + chr(8217) + 's numbers the Initial Fair Market Value is \$5,400,000, not \$8,000,000; (b) a fixed \$2,850,000 annuity sized to \$8,000,000 would be about 53% of the true value each year (present value about \$7.65M against a \$5.4M contribution).  ['Do not put any dollar funding value in the trust instrument. The draft defines the annuity as a percentage of the Initial Fair Market Value \"as finally determined for federal gift tax purposes\" (Art. III), so it self-corrects to whatever value is finally reported or determined.',

  '' + chr(8226) + ' Any fixed-dollar annuity is fragile here. If the IRS later values the shares higher, a fixed amount produces an unexpected gift. If the value is lower, a fixed amount over-pays the grantor.'],

# I. Purpose and Bottom Line

This memorandum accompanies Draft No. 1 of the Priya Chandrasekaran 2025 Grantor Retained Annuity Trust Agreement (grat-agreement.docx). It flags the problems we found across the seven source documents in the file (the May 20 intake memorandum, the May 22 engagement letter, the May 22 existing estate plan summary, the Ridgeline 409A valuation summary, the Silveroak projection workbook, the Helios Stockholders' Agreement Article IV excerpt, and Meg Hollister's May 28 email). Each of these must be resolved, or knowingly accepted, before the GRAT is funded.

**Bottom line:** The GRAT can be done, but not on the terms or the timetable the file currently assumes. Five problems would each defeat or materially impair the plan if not fixed:

- **The funding value is wrong.** Every planning document uses \$20.00 per share (\$8,000,000). Ridgeline's actual fair market value conclusion is **\$13.50 per share** (minority, non-marketable). \$20.00 is Ridgeline's pre-discount, marketable-control figure, which Ridgeline itself says \"should not be used\" as the fair market value of minority shares. On Ridgeline's numbers the 400,000 shares are worth **\$5,400,000**, and the \$13.50 figure is itself stale (Issues 1--2).

- **The annuity math is wrong.** Silveroak's 2.807 annuity factor is incorrect. The 3-year factor at 5.8% is 2.682934. - **The July 1, 2025 funding date cannot be met.** Section 4.2(a) of the Stockholders' Agreement requires a complete Trust Transfer Request **at least 60 days** before the transfer date. The Board then has a 30-day review period, and silence counts as a denial. A separate 30-day ROFR period follows Board consent. The intake memo, the engagement letter and the Silveroak workbook all describe only a 30-day process. The realistic funding window is mid-August to September 2025 (Issue 7).

- **Wheatley will not serve on the terms the client asked for.** Dr. Chandrasekaran wants day-to-day control as individual trustee. Wheatley requires exclusive authority over valuation, investment decisions and any discretion, and will decline the appointment otherwise. We go further and recommend that Wheatley also hold the vote of the Helios shares. Dr. Chandrasekaran owns exactly 20.0% of Helios's outstanding voting stock, which makes Helios a \"controlled corporation\" under IRC §2036(b) (Issues 10 and 13).

Dr. Chandrasekaran individually is not listed as a \"Permitted Transferee.\" Without an advance Board resolution, the trust may be unable to make an in-kind annuity payment within the 105-day grace period, and a missed payment would disqualify the annuity under §2702 (Issues 9 and 19).

I've drafted the zeroed-out GRAT agreement and an issues memo listing 27 problems that need resolving before funding. Both are .docx files in /workspace/output. I read all seven source documents in full, and both files pass the docx validator and parse back cleanly.

**The five problems that block funding:**
- **Wrong share value.** Every planning document funds at $20.00 a share ($8,000,000). That is Ridgeline's figure before discounts; its actual fair market value conclusion is $13.50 a share, or $5,400,000 for the 400,000 shares. Even $13.50 is out of date: the valuation date is March 31, 2025, before the May 8 Paramount licensing deal, and the report assumes no near-term IPO even though the board is in IPO talks.
- **Wrong annuity math.** Silveroak used an annuity factor of 2.807; the correct 3-year factor at 5.8% is 2.682934. The $2,850,000 annuity therefore creates a taxable gift of about $353,638, not the "$0.72" in the file. The draft uses a fixed percentage of the value as finally determined for gift tax (37.2726% at 5.8%, illustrative), so the gift stays near zero whatever value is finally used.
- **July 1, 2025 can't be met.** The stockholders' agreement requires the board consent request at least 60 days before transfer, then a 30-day board review where silence counts as denial, then a separate 30-day right of first refusal. The intake memo, engagement letter and Silveroak workbook all assume a single 30-day period. The memo recommends planning for September 2025.
- **Wheatley's conditions vs. the client's wishes.** Wheatley will decline the co-trustee role unless the client, as individual trustee, is limited to clerical tasks. That contradicts her request for day-to-day control. The draft also gives Wheatley sole voting power over the Helios shares, because she owns exactly 20.0% of the outstanding voting stock. At that level, voting the trust's shares as trustee risks pulling them back into her estate under §2036(b), or under §2035 if she dies within three years of giving up the vote.
- **Every later share movement is a restricted transfer.** That includes in-kind annuity payments back to her, asset swaps and the final distribution to the children. She is not on the agreement's list of permitted transferees, so the memo recommends one advance board resolution covering all of them. Without it, an annuity payment could miss the 105-day grace period, which would disqualify the GRAT.

**Other problems the memo covers:**
- The file uses 2024 tax figures: the 2025 lifetime exemption is $13.99M, not $13.61M, and the annual exclusion is $19,000, not $18,000.
- Her $8.2M of used exemption conflicts with Vikram's split-gift elections on the same gifts. If those gifts were split, her usage is about $5.95M.
- No document mentions the Connecticut gift tax return.
- The trust will hold only non-dividend stock, so it has no cash for Wheatley's fees or appraisals, and she can't pay them without making a prohibited extra contribution.
- No one has been assigned the securities opinion the board request requires.
- The intake memo and the 2017 revocable trust describe the fallback for a child who dies without descendants differently.
- Smaller items: Ridgeline describes the company's business differently from the intake memo, a distribution to a minor (Zara) needs handling, the power of attorney doesn't cover GRAT actions, and the engagement letter is unsigned.

**About the agreement:**
- The annuity continues to her estate for the full three years if she dies during the term; stopping it at death would create a taxable gift.
- Nothing goes into the trust before a single transfer of the shares, and only once board consent, the right-of-first-refusal waiver or lapse, and the trustees' joinders are in hand.
- Every trustee is bound to the stockholders' agreement, including the drag-along clause, as a condition of board consent.
- It includes an asset-swap power that keeps grantor trust status, a spendthrift clause and a holdback for minors.

**Decisions and things to check:**
- **Who gets the trust assets if she dies during the term.** Option A sends them to the children. Option B puts them in a marital trust for Vikram, which defers estate tax until his death.
- **Outright distribution or continuing trusts for the children.** Outright distribution leaves no creditor or divorce protection after the term ends.
- **Whether to put cash in alongside the shares** to cover fees and appraisals.
- **The 5.8% rate in the file isn't verified.** I couldn't check it against the IRS ruling offline. The final percentage must be set at signing using the lowest eligible month's rate.
- **The memo is dated June 2, 2025** to fit the file's timeline. If funding has actually slipped further, the rate and exemption figures need refreshing.

- issues-memorandum.docx
